s: Chapter 1 of Judith introduces Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians in Nineveh, and Arphaxad, king of the Medes in Ecbatana, whose city is described as fortified with massive walls, towers and gates. Nebuchadnezzar makes war on Arphaxad on the plain near Ragau and summons peoples from Persia, the west, Cilicia, Damascus, Samaria, Jerusalem and Egypt to join him. Those peoples disregard his summons and send his messengers away in disgrace, so Nebuchadnezzar swears by his throne and kingdom to take vengeance on them. In the seventeenth year he defeats Arphaxad's army, captures Ecbatana, plunders it, and kills Arphaxad with darts in the mountains of Ragau. He then returns to Nineveh with his multitude of soldiers and banquets for one hundred twenty days.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians in Nineveh, makes war on Arphaxad and sends summons to many western peoples, who refuse to join him. Angered, he swears by his throne and kingdom to avenge himself on them, then defeats Arphaxad in the seventeenth year, takes Ecbatana, and kills Arphaxad. He returns to Nineveh and feasts with his army for one hundred twenty days.

Arphaxad is introduced as king of the Medes in Ecbatana, who built the city's great walls, towers and gates for his army. Nebuchadnezzar defeats his army, horses and chariots, then captures him in the mountains of Ragau and strikes him through with darts, destroying him.

Ecbatana is the Median city of Arphaxad, fortified with hewn-stone walls seventy cubits high and fifty broad, towers a hundred cubits high, and gates seventy cubits high so the army could march out. Nebuchadnezzar takes its towers, plunders its streets, and turns its beauty into shame.

l: war between Nebuchadnezzar and Arphaxad, Judith, Judith / Chapter 1
s: The war is fought on the great plain on the borders of Ragau, with Arphaxad drawing allies from the hill country, the rivers, and the plain of Arioch king of the Elymaeans, and many nations of the sons of Chelod. In the seventeenth year Nebuchadnezzar prevails, routs Arphaxad's army, takes his cities including Ecbatana, and kills Arphaxad in the mountains of Ragau.

l: peoples of the western lands (Nebuchadnezzar's summoned), Judith, Judith / Chapter 1
s: Nebuchadnezzar sends messengers to peoples across Persia, Cilicia, Damascus, Libanus, the sea coast, Carmel, Gilead, Galilee, Esdraelon, Samaria, Jerusalem, and Egypt up to the borders of Ethiopia. They make light of his command, do not fear him, and turn his messengers away with disgrace, which provokes his oath of vengeance against Cilicia, Damascus, Syria, Moab, Ammon, Judea, and Egypt.

In the eighteenth year, Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians gathers his servants and great men, and they decree the destruction of all flesh that did not follow his word. He commissions Holofernes, his chief captain, to lead a vast army against the western country, demanding earth and water and ordering that resisters be slain and plundered. Holofernes musters 120,000 footmen and 12,000 mounted archers, with huge supplies of animals, rations, gold and silver, and sets out from Nineveh with a countless company of nations. His army destroys Put and Lud, crosses the Euphrates, ravages Mesopotamia, Cilicia, Midian and the plain of Damascus, and spreads fear among the coastal peoples of Sidon, Tyre, Sur, Ocina, Jemnaan, Azotus and Ascalon.

Nebuchadnezzar convenes his servants and great men, recounts the wickedness of the land, and they decree the destruction of all flesh that did not follow his word. He charges Holofernes with a campaign against the west, swearing by his life and kingdom that he will carry out his threats, including covering the earth with the feet of his army.

Holofernes, chief captain and second to the king, is commanded to go against the west country, take the coasts, spare those who yield and slay those who resist. He musters the army, leads it out from Nineveh, and conducts a campaign of destruction through many lands up to the sea coast.

The army consists of 120,000 chosen footmen and 12,000 mounted archers, with camels, donkeys, mules, countless livestock, rations, and gold and silver from the king's house. A countless company of various nations accompanies it like locusts, and it destroys, burns and plunders its way through many lands.

l: people of the west country, Judith, Chapter 2
s: The people of the west country are accused of disobeying the king's command and are to be told to prepare earth and water. Many are destroyed, including Put, Lud, the children of Rasses and Ishmael, and Midian, while the coastal cities of Sidon, Tyre, Sur, Ocina, Jemnaan, Azotus and Ascalon are seized by fear and dread.

l: Nebuchadnezzar's campaign of vengeance and conquest, Judith, Chapter 2
s: The campaign is decreed in the eighteenth year as vengeance on all the land. It begins from Nineveh toward Bectileth and Cilicia, crosses the Euphrates and Mesopotamia, burns Midian's tents and the fields of the plain of Damascus at wheat harvest, and reaches the sea coast, where its terror falls on the coastal cities.

Messengers are sent to Holofernes with words of peace, declaring that they are servants of Nebuchadnezzar the great king and offering him their dwellings, country, fields, flocks, herds and cities to use as he pleases. Holofernes comes down toward the sea coast with his army, sets garrisons in the high cities, and takes chosen men from them as allies. The people receive him with garlands, dances and timbrels. Despite this welcome, he casts down their borders and cuts down their sacred groves, having been given the task of destroying all the gods of the land so that all nations would worship Nebuchadnezzar only. He then moves toward Esdraelon near Dotaea, opposite the great ridge of Judea, and encamps between Geba and Scythopolis for a whole month to gather the baggage of his army.

Holofernes receives the messengers' words of submission and comes down toward the sea coast with his army, setting garrisons in the high cities and taking chosen men as allies. He is received with garlands, dances and timbrels, yet casts down borders and cuts down sacred groves, having been given the task of destroying all the gods of the land. He then advances toward Esdraelon near Dotaea, opposite the ridge of Judea, and camps between Geba and Scythopolis for a month to gather his army's baggage.

Nebuchadnezzar is called the great king, and the messengers describe their people as his servants. Holofernes has been given the task of destroying all the gods of the land so that all nations will worship Nebuchadnezzar only and all tongues and tribes will call upon him as a god.

The messengers are sent with words of peace to Holofernes. They carry a message that their people are servants of Nebuchadnezzar and that their dwellings, land, fields, flocks, herds and cities lie before him to be used as he pleases. They come to Holofernes and declare these words to him.

l: people of the coastal land (senders of the messengers), Judith, Chapter 3
s: The people send messengers to offer submission, and when Holofernes comes they receive him with garlands, dances and timbrels, along with all the country round about. Despite this, their borders are cast down and their sacred groves cut down, and garrisons are set in their high cities, from which chosen men are taken as allies.

l: submission of the messengers' people, Judith, Chapter 3
s: The people offer themselves, their dwellings, country, wheat fields, flocks, herds, tents and cities as servants of Nebuchadnezzar, to be dealt with as Holofernes sees fit. Holofernes accepts the offer by coming to their land, but it does not spare them from garrisons, conscription of allies, and the destruction of their borders and sacred groves.

l: campaign of destruction and worship of Nebuchadnezzar, Judith, Chapter 3
s: Holofernes casts down borders and cuts down sacred groves, carrying out his charge to destroy all the gods of the land. The stated aim is that all nations worship Nebuchadnezzar only and all their tongues and tribes call upon him as a god. The campaign then moves toward Esdraelon and the ridge of Judea, pausing a month at a camp between Geba and Scythopolis.

The children of Israel in Judea hear of all that Holofernes, chief captain of Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians, has done to the nations, and they fear for Jerusalem and the temple, which was recently re-sanctified after the captivity. They send word through Samaria and nearby places, occupy the mountaintops, fortify villages, and store supplies. Joakim the high priest writes to those in Bethulia and Betomesthaim to seize the ascents of the hill country, since the narrow approach there makes it easy to stop an invader, and the people and the senate obey. All Israel, including women, children, cattle, and servants, puts on sackcloth, prostrates before the temple, and cries to God not to give their families and sanctuary over to the nations. The Lord hears them, and the people keep fasting many days while Joakim and the priests, in sackcloth, offer the continual burnt offering and the people's vows and gifts.

Holofernes is identified as the chief captain of Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians. The people of Judea hear that he has plundered and utterly destroyed the temples of the nations, and his approach terrifies them.

The children of Israel in Judea fear Holofernes' approach, occupy the mountain tops, fortify villages, store supplies, and obey Joakim's command. They humble themselves in sackcloth, ashes, and fasting for many days, crying to God with one consent not to let their families and sanctuary be given to the nations.

Judea is where the children of Israel live, newly returned from captivity and recently gathered. Its entrance is through the hill-country ascents, and the whole land keeps fasting for many days before the sanctuary.

Jerusalem is the seat of Joakim the high priest and of the senate of all the people of Israel, whose members carry out his command. Its inhabitants fall prostrate before the temple in sackcloth and ashes, and they join the fasting.

l: house of God (Jerusalem sanctuary), Judith, Chapter 4
s: The temple, with its vessels, altar, and house, had been sanctified after being profaned, and the people fear for it. They fall prostrate before it, put sackcloth around the altar, and pray that the sanctuary not be profaned and made a reproach. Joakim and the priests offer the continual burnt offering, vows, and free gifts there.
The Lord, called God of Israel and Lord Almighty, is the one to whom all Israel cries with earnestness. He hears their voice and looks at their affliction.

Joakim the high priest at Jerusalem writes to those in Bethulia and Betomesthaim, charging them to seize the ascents of the hill country, and the people obey. He and the priests dress in sackcloth, wear ashes on their turbans, offer the continual burnt offering, vows, and free gifts, and cry to the Lord to look on Israel for good.

The ascents are the entrance into Judea, and Joakim orders them seized because the approach is narrow, with space for two men at most, making it easy to stop an invader. The children of Israel do as he commanded.

Sackcloth is put on the loins of the people, their wives, children, cattle, sojourners, hirelings, and servants, and is spread out before the Lord and placed around the altar. Joakim and the priests also wear it as a sign of humbling.

All Israel cries to God earnestly and with one consent, with ashes on their heads, that their children, wives, cities, and sanctuary not be given to destruction or reproach. The Lord hears, and the people continue fasting many days in Judea and Jerusalem before the sanctuary.

Holofernes, chief captain of the army of Asshur, learns that the children of Israel have fortified the hill country and prepared for war, and he angrily demands that the princes of Moab, the captains of Ammon, and the governors of the sea coast explain who these people are. Achior, leader of the children of Ammon, answers by recounting Israel's history: their descent from the Chaldeans, their worship of the God of heaven, their sojourns in Mesopotamia, Canaan, and Egypt, their deliverance through the Red Sea, and their conquest of the hill country. He explains that they prospered while they did not sin and were destroyed and taken captive when they left God's way, and that they have now returned to their God and resettled Jerusalem. Achior advises Holofernes to attack only if the people have sinned, and otherwise to pass by, lest their God defend them. The people around the tent complain, and Holofernes' great men and those of Moab and the sea coast say Achior should be cut to pieces, claiming Israel has no power or might and will be prey for the army.

Holofernes, chief captain of the army of Asshur, is told that Israel has fortified the hill country and prepared for war, and he becomes exceedingly angry. He questions the princes of Moab, the captains of Ammon, and the governors of the sea coast about the people, their cities, army, strength, and king. He hears Achior's advice, and his great men urge attacking, calling Israel prey to be devoured by his army.

Achior, leader of all the children of Ammon, promises to tell Holofernes the truth and gives a full history of Israel from the Chaldeans through Egypt, the Red Sea, and the conquest of the hill country. He advises that Holofernes attack only if Israel has sinned against its God, and otherwise pass by. His words provoke complaint, and Holofernes' great men and those of Moab and the sea coast say he should be cut to pieces.

The children of Israel are reported to have shut up the passages of the hill country, fortified the high hilltops, and set up barricades in the plains. Achior describes them as descended from the Chaldeans, having left their fathers' gods to worship the God of heaven, and having sojourned in Mesopotamia, Canaan, and Egypt. They were enslaved in Egypt, freed, and took the hill country, were later taken captive for leaving God's way, and have now returned and settled Jerusalem. Holofernes' men dismiss them as having no power or might.

Achior says the God of heaven commanded the Israelites to leave Mesopotamia for Canaan, struck Egypt with incurable plagues, dried up the Red Sea before them, and cast out the peoples before them. He is described as one who hates iniquity and was with Israel while they did not sin. Achior warns that if Israel is without lawlessness, their Lord and God will defend them and Holofernes' army would be a reproach before all the earth.

The hill country is where Israel has shut up the passages and fortified the high hilltops, near where Holofernes is. Achior says Israel possessed all of it after crossing the Jordan and again settled in it after returning from dispersion, because it was desolate. Holofernes' men say they will go up against it and make Israel prey.

l: Israelite sin and its consequences, Judith, Chapter 5
s: Achior teaches that Israel prospered while it did not sin before its God, because God who hates iniquity was with them. When they departed from the way he appointed, they were destroyed in many severe battles, led captive into a land not theirs, their temple was razed, and their cities were taken. He proposes that Holofernes find out whether they now stumble in sin before attacking, and pass by if there is no lawlessness among them.

After the council uproar subsides, Holofernes, chief captain of Asshur's army, mocks Achior and the Moabites for prophesying that Israel's God will defend Israel, declares that Nebuchadnezzar is the only god, and vows that Israel will be destroyed. He orders his servants to take Achior to Bethulia and hand him over to the children of Israel, so that Achior will share their fate. The servants bring Achior to the springs below Bethulia, where slingers drive them off, and they bind him and leave him at the foot of the hill. The Israelites free him and bring him to the city's rulers, Ozias, Chabris, and Charmis, and Achior reports Holofernes' words to the assembly. The people worship and pray to God, comfort and praise Achior, and Ozias hosts him and the elders at a feast while they call on God all night.

Holofernes, chief captain of Asshur's army, rebukes Achior before the assembled people, scorns Israel's God, and asserts that Nebuchadnezzar is the only god and that Israel will perish. He sentences Achior to be delivered to the Israelites so that he will be destroyed with them, and commands his servants to take him to Bethulia.

Achior is denounced by Holofernes as a hireling of Ammon for his prophecy that Israel's God will defend Israel, and is sent to Bethulia to share the fate of the Israelites. He is bound and left at the foot of the hill, freed by the Israelites, and brought before Ozias and the city's rulers, where he recounts Holofernes' words. The people comfort and praise him, and Ozias takes him into his house.

Nebuchadnezzar is called by Holofernes the lord of all the earth and the only god, who will send forth his might to destroy Israel. Holofernes quotes him as saying his spoken words will not be in vain.

Bethulia is the city whose men, seeing Holofernes' servants on the hilltop, take up weapons and use slingers to keep them from coming up. It receives the freed Achior and gathers its elders, young men, and women in assembly, led by the rulers Ozias, Chabris, and Charmis.

The children of Israel descend from Bethulia, untie Achior, lead him into the city, and present him to their rulers. After hearing Holofernes' threats they fall down, worship God, and pray for pity on their low estate. They comfort and praise Achior and call on God all night.

The God of Israel is mocked by Holofernes, who says he will not deliver his people from Nebuchadnezzar's might. The people of Bethulia address him as Lord God of heaven, ask him to see the arrogance of their enemies and pity them, and call on him for help all night.
Ozias, son of Micah of the tribe of Simeon, is named as one of Bethulia's three rulers. He asks Achior what happened, then takes him from the assembly into his house and makes a feast for the elders.

Holofernes' servants are commanded to take Achior to Bethulia and deliver him to the Israelites. They bring him to the springs below the city, are driven back by slingers, then bind Achior, leave him at the foot of the hill, and return to their lord.

Holofernes orders his huge army to move against Bethulia, where it camps in the valley and seizes the passes. The children of Israel are terrified and keep watch all night. Holofernes inspects the ascents and springs, and the rulers of Esau, Moab and the sea coast advise him to besiege the city and cut off its water rather than fight. He agrees, and the Ammonites, Assyrians and Esau's children take the springs and surround the city. After thirty-four days the cisterns are dry and the people, faint with thirst, demand that Ozias surrender; he asks for five more days for God to show mercy, and promises to yield if no help comes.

Holofernes commands his army and allies to move against Bethulia and seize the passes of the hill country. He rides out with his cavalry to view the ascents and the springs, posts garrisons over the springs, and then accepts the advice of the rulers of Esau, Moab and the sea coast to besiege the city rather than fight, ordering them to do as they proposed.

The army, numbering one hundred seventy thousand footmen and twelve thousand horsemen besides baggage, camps in the valley by the fountain near Bethulia and spreads over a vast area. Part of it, including five thousand children of Asshur who go with the Ammonites, seizes the waters and springs, and the rest covers the plain. It remains around Bethulia for thirty-four days.

Bethulia is surrounded by the enemy host, which seizes the springs below it and the ascents to it. Over thirty-four days its cisterns empty and its people collapse in the streets and gate passages from thirst. It is brought very low, with its walls and towers still manned.

The children of Israel are terrified at the sight of the enemy multitude, take up their weapons, light fires on their towers and watch all night. Besieged and without escape, they cry to the Lord their God. As thirst weakens them, the people turn on their rulers, demanding surrender, before agreeing to wait five more days.

Ozias, one of the city's rulers, is confronted by the whole people, who blame him and the other rulers for not seeking peace with the Assyrians. He urges courage and asks for five more days for the Lord to turn his mercy toward them. He promises to do as the people say if no help comes, then disperses them to their posts and sends the women and children home.

Their rulers, together with the leaders of Moab and the captains of the sea coast, advise Holofernes that Israel trusts in its mountain heights and should be starved of water rather than fought. Their plan is adopted, and the children of Esau go up with the Ammonites and camp in the hill country near Dothaim, sending some toward the south and east.

The besieged children of Israel cry out to the Lord their God in their distress and weeping. The people say God has sold them into enemy hands and punishes them for their sins and their fathers' sins. Ozias says the Lord will turn his mercy toward them and will not forsake them utterly.

l: water springs of Bethulia, Judith, Chapter 7
s: The springs, including the one flowing from the foot of the mountain, supply all the inhabitants of Bethulia. Holofernes searches them out and garrisons them, and the Ammonites and Assyrians then seize them, cutting off the city's water.

Following the advice of Esau's and Moab's leaders, Holofernes besieges Bethulia, seizing the springs and occupying the nearby hills so that no one can leave. After thirty-four days the water has run out and the people demand surrender. Ozias secures a delay of five days, promising to surrender if no help comes.

Judith, a wealthy and devout widow of Bethulia whose husband Manasses died during barley harvest, hears that Ozias has sworn to deliver the city to the Assyrians after five days if God does not help. She summons Ozias, Chabris, and Charmis and rebukes them for testing God and putting themselves in his place, urging the people to wait for God's salvation and to see the trial as discipline like that of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Ozias praises her wisdom but says the thirsty people forced the oath and asks her to pray for rain. Judith replies that she will do a deed remembered through all generations, instructs them to stand at the gate that night, and forbids them to inquire about it. Ozias and the rulers bless her and return to their stations.

Judith is introduced as the daughter of Merari and widow of Manasses, living three years and four months in widowhood in a roof tent with sackcloth and fasting, beautiful, wealthy, and with no evil said of her because she feared God. She summons the elders, rebukes them for testing God with the oath, and tells them she will go out with her maid and that the Lord will deliver Israel by her hand within the appointed days, without revealing her act.

Bethulia is the city of Judith and of her late husband Manasses, whose people are fainting from lack of water. Its leaders have sworn to surrender it to the Assyrians after five days, and Judith warns that its capture would mean the capture of all Judea and the plundering of the sanctuary.

Ozias had sworn to the people that he would deliver the city to the Assyrians after five days. When Judith rebukes him, he acknowledges her wisdom and good heart, explains that the thirsty people compelled the oath, asks her to pray for rain, and then blesses her and sends her off in peace.

Ozias, Chabris, and Charmis, the elders of the city, are summoned by Judith's maid and are told that their word before the people was not right. They accept her commission, agree not to inquire into her act, say 'Go in peace,' and return to their stations.

God is described by Judith as Lord Almighty, whose mind cannot be searched out and who cannot be threatened or won over like a human being. He may help or destroy at the time he chooses, and he tries and scourges those near him to admonish them, as he did with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Judith says he will deliver Israel by her hand.

The Assyrians are the enemies to whom Ozias has promised to deliver Bethulia after five days. Judith warns that falling to them would bring captivity, plunder of the sanctuary, and dishonor on the people.

Ozias's oath to deliver the city to the Assyrians after five days unless God helps is condemned by Judith as wrongly placed between God and the leaders, and as testing God. Ozias defends it as forced by the thirsty people and says it cannot be broken, so Judith works within its time limit.

Judith announces a deed that will be remembered through all generations, in which she will go out of the city gate with her maid and the Lord will deliver Israel by her hand within the days set by the oath. She forbids the rulers to inquire about it and says she will tell them only once it is finished.

Judith falls on her face, puts ashes on her head, and uncovers her sackcloth as the evening incense is offered at Jerusalem, then cries out to the Lord. She recalls how the Lord gave her father Simeon a sword to avenge a violated virgin, and asks to be heard as a widow. She describes the Assyrians as proud, trusting in horses, riders, footmen, shield, spear, bow, and sling, and as intending to defile the sanctuary and destroy the horn of the altar. She asks God to break their strength, to strike servant and prince by the deceit of her lips, and to use the hand of a woman. She closes by asking that every nation and tribe know that no one but the Lord protects the race of Israel.

Judith falls on her face, puts ashes on her head, uncovers her sackcloth, and cries loudly to the Lord at the hour of the evening incense. She identifies herself as a widow and asks God to give into her hand the might she has conceived. She asks that her speech and deceit become a wound to those who plan harm against God's covenant and house.

The Lord is addressed as the God of Simeon, who gave him a sword to take vengeance and gave the defilers' rulers, wives, daughters, and spoils into Israel's hands. He is described as having planned past, present, and future things, as a God of the afflicted, helper of the oppressed and weak, protector of the forsaken, and savior of the hopeless. Judith asks him to break the Assyrians' strength and to show all nations that no one else protects Israel.

The Assyrians are described as multiplied in power, exalted with horse and rider, proud of their footmen, and trusting in shield, spear, bow, and sling. They do not know that the Lord breaks battles. Judith says they intend to profane the sanctuary, defile the tabernacle, and destroy the horn of the altar with the sword.

Israel is called the inheritance of God, and its race is said to be protected by the Lord alone. Its holy house, the top of Zion, and the covenant are named as the things the Assyrians threaten. Judith recalls that in the past God's dear children, moved with zeal for him, received the spoils of those who defiled a virgin.

The prayer recalls Simeon's vengeance, affirms God's foreknowledge and his care for the weak, and describes the Assyrian threat. It petitions God to break the Assyrians through the deceit of her lips and the hand of a woman. It ends by asking that every nation and tribe know that the Lord is God and Israel's only protector.

After finishing her prayer, Judith removes her widow's garments and sackcloth, bathes, and dresses in her finest clothing and jewelry to make herself very beautiful. With her maid, carrying wine, oil, roasted grain, figs, and bread, she goes to the gate of Bethulia, where Ozias, Chabris, and Charmis bless her and have the gate opened. In the valley an Assyrian watch stops her, and she says she is a Hebrew fleeing because her people are about to be consumed, and that she will show Holofernes a way to win the hill country. Struck by her beauty, the Assyrians send a hundred men to escort her to the tent of Holofernes, and the whole camp gathers around her. Holofernes comes out with silver lamps before him, and Judith bows down to him before his servants raise her up.

Judith rises from prayer, discards her widow's clothing, and dresses beautifully, then leaves Bethulia with her maid after the elders bless her. Stopped by an Assyrian watch, she says she is a Hebrew fleeing her people and that she will show Holofernes how to win the hill country without losing a man. She is escorted to his tent, and bows before him until his servants raise her up.

Holofernes is called the chief captain of the Assyrian army, and Judith says she is coming to him with words of truth. He is resting on a bed under a canopy woven with purple, gold, emeralds, and precious stones when told of her arrival. He comes out before his tent with silver lamps going before him and receives Judith.

Bethulia is a city with a gate, at which Ozias and the elders Chabris and Charmis stand. They open it for Judith and her maid, and the men of the city watch her until she goes down the mountain and passes the valley out of sight.

The elders pray that Judith's purposes will bring glory to the children of Israel and exaltation to Jerusalem. The Assyrians, seeing Judith, marvel at the children of Israel because they have such women among them, and say that if they are let go they could deceive the whole earth.

An Assyrian watch meets Judith in the valley, questions her, and is amazed by her beauty. They tell her she has saved her life, and send a hundred men to escort her to Holofernes' tent. The camp is greatly excited and surrounds her, and Holofernes' guards and servants bring her into the tent and marvel at her face.

Judith washes, anoints herself with rich ointment, braids her hair, puts on a tiara, her garments of gladness from the days of Manasses her husband, sandals, an anklet, bracelets, rings, earrings, and all her jewelry. The purpose stated is to make herself very beautiful to deceive the eyes of all men who see her. It astonishes the elders, the Assyrian watch, the camp, and Holofernes' servants.

Holofernes reassures Judith that she will be safe and well treated if she has chosen to serve Nebuchadnezzar, and asks why she fled her people. Judith flatters him and claims that her people can only be defeated if they sin against their God. She says they have run short of food and water and mean to eat livestock and the sanctified first fruits, tithes of wine and oil, and that they have sent to Jerusalem for the elders' permission. She claims that once they do this they will be delivered to Holofernes, and she offers to stay, pray at night in the valley for a sign of their sin, and then lead him through Judea to Jerusalem. Holofernes and his servants are pleased and amazed by her beauty and wisdom, and Holofernes promises that if she does as she says, her God will be his God and she will dwell in Nebuchadnezzar's palace.

Holofernes tells Judith to take courage and promises that anyone who serves Nebuchadnezzar will not be harmed, blaming her people for the attack on them. He is pleased by her words, praises her beauty and wisdom, and promises that if she does as she says, her God will be his God and she will live in Nebuchadnezzar's palace.

Judith speaks to Holofernes, flattering him and claiming that she will not lie to him. She says she fled her people because of their coming sin, offers to pray in the valley each night to learn when they sin, and promises to lead him to Jerusalem and set his throne there. She is praised by Holofernes and his servants as unmatched in beauty and wisdom.

Nebuchadnezzar is called king of all the earth, and Holofernes says those who serve him will not be hurt. Judith claims that even the beasts and birds live through his power and Holofernes' strength. Holofernes offers her a home in his palace and renown throughout the earth.

Jerusalem is where the priests stand before God, and Judith says the Bethulians have sent people there to get permission from the council of elders to consume the sanctified food. She claims that people there have done the same thing. She promises to lead Holofernes through Judea to Jerusalem and set his throne in its midst.

Judith says her people will not be punished and the sword will not prevail against them unless they sin against their God. She claims that, with food and water running short, they plan to kill their livestock and eat what is sanctified, and that they will then be delivered to Holofernes to be destroyed. Holofernes says they slighted him and brought their troubles on themselves.

Judith says God will bring things to pass perfectly with Holofernes and that he sent her to work things that will astonish all the earth. She says she serves the God of heaven day and night and that he will tell her when her people have sinned. Holofernes says God did well to send her and promises that her God will become his God.

l: Israelites' sin of consuming sanctified food, Judith, Chapter 11
s: Judith claims that, because their food and water have failed, her people mean to kill their livestock and eat what God forbade them by his laws, including first fruits of the grain and tithes of wine and oil reserved for the priests. She says they have sought permission from the elders in Jerusalem and that, once they act, they will be given over to Holofernes to be destroyed the same day.

Holofernes has Judith brought to where his silver vessels are set and offers her his own food and wine, but she declines, saying her own provisions will suffice until the Lord works through her hand. She stays in the camp three days, going out each night to the valley of Bethulia to wash at the fountain and pray that God direct her way. On the fourth day Holofernes holds a feast for his servants only and sends Bagoas the eunuch to persuade her to join them. Judith agrees, dresses in her finery, and sits on fleeces laid out beside Holofernes, who is captivated and has desired her since first seeing her. She eats and drinks what her servant prepared, and Holofernes, delighted, drinks more wine than he ever had in a single day.

Judith refuses Holofernes' food and wine, saying her own provisions will be used until the Lord works by her hand. She stays three days in the camp, going out each night to wash at the fountain and pray, then accepts the invitation to the feast through Bagoas, dresses in her finery, and sits beside Holofernes. She says her life is magnified in her that day and eats and drinks only what her servant prepared.

Holofernes offers Judith his own delicacies and wine, orders his guards not to stop her nightly outings, and on the fourth day holds a feast for his servants only. He sends Bagoas to bring her, is ravished by her and had been watching for a time to deceive her since first seeing her. At the feast he delights in her and drinks more wine than on any previous day of his life.

Bagoas is the eunuch who has charge over all that Holofernes has. Holofernes sends him to persuade Judith to come eat and drink with them, and he tells her not to fear and that she will be honored like the daughters of Asshur who serve in Nebuchadnezzar's palace. Judith accepts, and she had received the fleeces for her daily use from him.

On the fourth day Holofernes makes a feast for his own servants only, calling none of the officers. Judith attends at his invitation via Bagoas, sits on fleeces beside him, and eats and drinks what her servant prepared. Holofernes grows delighted and drinks exceedingly much wine, more than on any day since his birth.

l: Judith's food and provisions, Judith, Chapter 12
s: Judith declines Holofernes' delicacies and wine, saying she cannot eat them lest there be an occasion of stumbling, and that provision will be made from what came with her. When Holofernes asks what will happen when it runs out, she says it will not be used up until the Lord works by her hand. She eats her food toward evening each day and at the feast eats and drinks what her servant prepared.

In the evening, after a long feast, Bagoas shuts the tent and the servants leave Judith alone with Holofernes, who lies drunk on his bed. Judith prays to the Lord God, takes Holofernes' sword from the bedpost, and cuts off his head with two blows to the neck. She gives the head to her maid, who puts it in the food bag, and the two pass through the camp as if going to prayer and reach the gates of Bethulia. Judith announces God's victory to the watchmen and the gathered people, shows the head and the canopy, and says Holofernes did not defile her. The people worship God, and Ozias blesses Judith above all women and praises her for not sparing her life for her people.

Judith, left alone in the tent with the drunk Holofernes, prays for strength, takes his sword, and cuts off his head with two blows. She leaves with her maid, carrying the head in the food bag, passes through the camp and reaches the gates of Bethulia, where she announces that God has destroyed the enemies by her hand and shows the head. Ozias blesses her above all women, and the people say "Amen! Amen!" to his praise.

Holofernes lies drunk on his bed in the tent after the long feast, with his servants gone. Judith cuts off his head with his own sword and tumbles his body from the bed. She calls him the chief captain of the army of Asshur and says the Lord struck him by the hand of a woman, and that he did not sin with her.

God is addressed by Judith as "O Lord God of all power" and "O Lord God of Israel" when she prays for help and strength before the deed. Judith, the people and Ozias credit him with the victory, saying he showed his power in Israel, did not take away his mercy from the house of Israel, and humiliated the enemies of his people. The people worship him, and Ozias calls him creator of the heavens and the earth who directed Judith to cut off the enemy prince's head.

Judith and her maid go up the mountain to Bethulia and reach its gates, where Judith calls to the watchmen to open. The men of the city hurry down, call the elders, and everyone, small and great, runs together, finding her return unbelievable. They open the gate, light a fire, and surround the women, then worship God and bless Judith after she shows the head.

Holofernes' head is given by Judith to her maid after it is cut off and is put in her bag of food. At the gate of Bethulia, Judith takes it from the bag and shows it to the people as proof that the enemy captain is dead. The people are amazed and worship God.

Judith carries out the beheading while Holofernes lies drunk on his bed, after praying for help and strength. She takes hold of his hair and strikes twice on his neck with all her might, cutting off his head. She then tumbles the body from the bed and takes down the canopy, which she later shows to the people along with the head.

Judith tells her kindred to hang Holofernes' head on the city wall and instructs them to arm themselves at dawn and feign a descent toward the Assyrian watch, so that the Assyrians will rouse their captains, fail to find Holofernes, flee, and be pursued across Israel. She has Achior the Ammonite summoned; he faints at the sight of the head, then bows to her, hears her account of her deeds, and comes to believe in God, is circumcised, and joins the house of Israel. At morning the people hang the head on the wall and go out in bands to the mountain ascents. The Assyrians send word to their leaders, who come to Holofernes' tent, and Bagoas enters and finds Holofernes dead and headless on the threshold. Bagoas finds Judith gone, cries out that a Hebrew woman has shamed the house of King Nebuchadnezzar, and the Assyrian camp falls into uproar and mourning.

Judith instructs her kindred to hang Holofernes' head on the wall and lays out a plan to make the Assyrians flee, which the Israelites will then pursue. She has Achior summoned and tells the assembled people everything she has done from the day she went out until she spoke to them, and the people shout and rejoice. Achior bows at her feet and blesses her, and Bagoas later finds her gone from her lodging and the Assyrians blame her for the shame on Nebuchadnezzar's house.

Holofernes is found dead by Bagoas, cast upon the threshold of the bedchamber with his head taken from him. The Assyrian rulers are told he lies on the ground headless, and the camp is thrown into turmoil. Achior is brought to see the man who despised Israel and sent him to the Israelites as if to his death.

Judith has the head hung on the battlement of the wall, and it is displayed in the assembly of the people, where it makes Achior faint. At morning it is hanged upon the wall, and the Assyrians' discovery that it has been taken from the body sparks their alarm.

Summoned from the house of Ozias, Achior sees Holofernes' head, falls on his face, and his spirit fails. After reviving he bows at Judith's feet, blesses her, and asks to hear what she did. Having seen what the God of Israel had done, he believes in God exceedingly, is circumcised, and is joined to the house of Israel to this day.

Bagoas goes to Holofernes' tent, knocks, and supposes Holofernes is sleeping with Judith. Getting no answer, he enters, finds Holofernes dead and headless, weeps and tears his garments, and discovers Judith's lodging empty. He cries out to the people that one Hebrew woman has shamed the house of King Nebuchadnezzar.

Israel is the people whose house Achior joins, and Judith says all who inhabit its borders shall pursue and overthrow the fleeing Assyrians. Achior says that those in every nation who hear Judith's name will be troubled. The Assyrians call the Israelites slaves who have dealt treacherously.

Judith's kindred are told to hang the head on the wall and to arm themselves at dawn and go out as if descending to the plain, without actually going down. They shout and rejoice when Judith finishes her account, then hang the head and go out by bands to the mountain ascents with their weapons.

The children of Asshur see the Israelites coming and send word to their leaders, who go to the captains and tribunes and then to Holofernes' tent to ask that he be woken. On learning of his death, the rulers of the army tear their tunics, are exceedingly troubled, and a great cry and noise arises in the camp. Judith had predicted fear would fall on them and that they would flee.

l: Israelite attack on the Assyrian camp, Judith, Chapter 14
s: Judith lays out the plan: at morning the men take up arms and go out with a captain as though going down to the plain, but do not descend. The Assyrians would rouse their captains, find Holofernes missing, and flee, and Israel would pursue them. In this unit the Israelites go out in bands to the mountain ascents, and the Assyrians see them and take them to be coming down to battle, while the attack itself has not yet been carried out.

Those in the enemy tents hear what has happened, are seized with fear, and flee across the plain and hill country. Ozias sends word to Betomasthaim, Bebai, Chobai, Chola, and every border of Israel, and the children of Israel, joined by people from Jerusalem, Gilead, and Galilee, pursue and slaughter the enemy past Damascus. The people of Bethulia plunder the camp of Asshur and are greatly enriched, and the villages and cities of the hill country and plain also take many spoils. Joakim the high priest and the elders from Jerusalem come to see Judith, bless her as the glory of Israel, and the people answer 'Amen.' After thirty days of plunder, Holofernes' tent and furnishings are given to Judith, and she leads the women of Israel in a dance with olive garlands while the armed men follow singing.

Judith is visited by Joakim the high priest and the elders from Jerusalem, who bless her as the exaltation of Jerusalem, the glory of Israel, and the rejoicing of her race, saying she did these things by her hand. She is given Holofernes' tent, silver cups, beds, bowls, and furniture, which she loads on her mule and wagons. She distributes branches to the women and leads all the women in the dance, wearing an olive garland, with the men following.

The children of Israel, every warrior among them, rush out upon the fleeing enemy, and when they hear Ozias's message they fall upon them with one accord and strike them to Chobai. They return from the slaughter, take possession of what remains, and take many spoils. At the end they follow Judith in armor and garlands, singing.

The camp of Asshur is thrown into trembling and fear when those in the tents hear what has happened, and its people flee into every way of the plain and hill country. Those who had encamped around Bethulia flee, and the enemy is slaughtered past Damascus and its borders. Its camp is plundered and enriches the Israelites exceedingly.
The enemy who had encamped in the hill country round about Bethulia flee away. The rest of the people who lived at Bethulia fall upon the camp of Asshur and plunder it, becoming exceedingly enriched.

The people of Bethulia plunder the camp of Asshur and are enriched exceedingly, and villages and cities in the hill country and plain take many spoils from an exceedingly great supply. The people plunder the camp for thirty days. Holofernes' tent, silver cups, beds, bowls, and furniture are given to Judith.

All the women of Israel run together to see Judith, bless her, and make a dance for her. Judith gives branches to the women, and she and those with her make garlands of olive. She leads all the women in the dance, and all the men of Israel follow in armor with garlands and songs in their mouths.

l: pursuit and slaughter of the enemy, Judith, Chapter 15
s: After the enemy flees, the Israelite warriors rush upon them, and Ozias sends word to Betomasthaim, Bebai, Chobai, Chola, and every border of Israel to destroy the enemy. The Israelites strike them to Chobai, and people from Jerusalem, the hill country, Gilead, and Galilee fall on their flank with great slaughter until they are past Damascus and its borders.

Judith leads all Israel in a song of thanksgiving, recounting how the Lord destroyed Asshur's vast army by the hand of a woman, as she used her beauty and a deception to make the enemy leader weak and strike his neck with the sword. The song praises the Lord as creator and merciful to those who fear him, and warns that nations rising against Israel will suffer judgment. On reaching Jerusalem, the people worship, are purified, and offer burnt offerings, free will offerings, and gifts, while Judith dedicates Holofernes' belongings and the canopy to the Lord. After three months of feasting, Judith returns to Bethulia, remains unmarried and honored, frees her maid, and dies at 105, buried in the cave of her husband Manasses and mourned for seven days. No one frightened Israel during her days or for a long time after.

Judith begins and leads a song of thanksgiving in which she credits the Lord with using her beauty to weaken the enemy's mighty one. She dedicates Holofernes' belongings and the canopy to the Lord, returns to Bethulia, and is honored, though no man knew her after her husband Manasses died. She frees her maid, distributes her goods to kin, dies at 105, and is buried in Manasses' cave.

The Lord is praised in Judith's song as the God who crushes battles, delivered her from persecutors, and brought Asshur's army to nothing by the hand of a woman. He is described as great, glorious, invincible, creator of all by his spoken word and spirit, merciful to those who fear him, and a future avenger who will judge hostile nations. The people worship him in Jerusalem and receive offerings and Judith's gifts.

Asshur is described in Judith's song as coming from the northern mountains with ten thousands of his army, stopping torrents with its multitude. He is said to have threatened to burn Israel's borders, kill young men, and take infants and virgins as prey. The Almighty Lord brought him to nothing by the hand of a woman.

Holofernes is not named in the song, but the text calls the enemy's mighty one one who fell not by young men, Titans, or giants but was made weak by Judith's beauty and struck through the neck with the sword. Afterward his belongings, given to Judith by the people, are dedicated to the Lord, and his canopy, taken from his bedchamber, is given as a gift.

Israel sings loudly along with Judith in praise, and its lowly, oppressed people shouted, trembled, and saw the enemy flee. The people worship and offer sacrifices in Jerusalem, feast for three months, and return to their inheritances. The house of Israel mourns Judith seven days, and no one makes them afraid in her days or long after.

The army is described as vast, with ten thousands of men and horsemen covering the hills. When Israel's lowly ones shouted, the enemy fled, and the children of slave-girls pierced them through, so they perished by the army of the Lord. The Persians and Medes are said to have quaked at Judith's daring.

l: Judith's song of thanksgiving, Judith, Chapter 16
s: Judith begins the song in all Israel, and all the people sing it with loud voices. It calls for timbrels and cymbals, recounts the defeat of Asshur by a woman, praises the Lord as great creator and merciful to those who fear him, and ends by warning that nations against Israel will suffer fire and worms in judgment.

Psalm 1 contrasts the blessed man with the wicked. The blessed man avoids the counsel of the wicked, the path of sinners, and the seat of scoffers, and instead delights in the LORD's law and meditates on it day and night. He is compared to a tree planted by streams of water that bears fruit in season, whose leaf does not wither, and whatever he does prospers. The wicked are compared to chaff driven away by the wind, and they will not stand in the judgment or in the congregation of the righteous. The LORD knows the way of the righteous, while the way of the wicked will perish.

l: the man (the blessed man), Psalms, Psalms / Chapter 1
s: The blessed man does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, stand on the path of sinners, or sit in the seat of scoffers. His delight is in the LORD's law, on which he meditates day and night. He is likened to a tree planted by streams of water that yields fruit in season and whose leaf does not wither, and whatever he does prospers.

The wicked are described as not like the blessed man but like chaff that the wind drives away. They will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous, and their way will perish.
The righteous have a congregation in which sinners will not be able to stand. The LORD knows their way.
The LORD is the one whose law the blessed man delights in and meditates on. He knows the way of the righteous, while the way of the wicked perishes.

l: law (the LORD's law), Psalms, Psalms / Chapter 1
s: The LORD's law is the object of the blessed man's delight, and he meditates on it day and night. Delight in it is part of what marks the man as blessed.

Chapter 2 opens by asking why the nations and peoples rage and plot in vain. The kings and rulers of the earth take counsel together against the LORD and his Anointed, resolving to break their bonds and cast off their cords. The LORD, sitting in the heavens, laughs at them in derision, then speaks in anger and wrath, declaring that he has set his King on his holy hill of Zion. A speaker relates the LORD's decree that he is his son, who is promised the nations as an inheritance and the ends of the earth as a possession, and who will break them with a rod of iron. The chapter closes by urging the kings and judges to be wise, serve the LORD with fear, and give homage to the Son lest they perish, while blessing all who take refuge in him.

The LORD sits in the heavens and laughs in derision at the kings who plot against him and his Anointed. He then speaks to them in anger and wrath, saying he has set his King on his holy hill of Zion. He also decrees to the speaker, "You are my son. Today I have become your father," and promises him the nations and the ends of the earth.

The Anointed is the target of the kings' and rulers' plotting alongside the LORD. He is identified as the King the LORD has set on Zion, and as the son to whom the LORD gives the nations as an inheritance and the earth's far reaches as a possession. He is to break the nations with a rod of iron and dash them like a potter's vessel, and the kings are told to give homage to the Son, lest his wrath be kindled; those who take refuge in him are blessed.

The nations are described as raging, and the peoples as plotting a vain thing. The LORD promises them to his son as an inheritance, and they are to be broken with a rod of iron and dashed in pieces like a potter's vessel.

l: kings of the earth, Psalms, Chapter 2
s: The kings of the earth take a stand and, with the rulers, take counsel together against the LORD and his Anointed, wanting to break their bonds apart. They are then called to be wise and instructed, to serve the LORD with fear and rejoice with trembling, and to give sincere homage to the Son lest they perish on the way.

l: rebellion against the LORD, Psalms, Chapter 2
s: The rebellion is the plot of the nations, peoples, kings and rulers to break apart the bonds and cast off the cords of the LORD and his Anointed. It is called vain, and the LORD answers it with laughter, derision, anger and wrath, and by setting his King on Zion. The text warns that those who persist will perish, while those who take refuge in the Son are blessed.

Chapter 3 is a psalm by David, written when he fled from his son Absalom. David laments that his adversaries have multiplied and that many say there is no help for him in God. He affirms that the LORD is his shield, his glory, and the one who lifts up his head, and that the LORD answers his cry from his holy hill. David says he lay down, slept, and woke because the LORD sustains him, so he will not fear tens of thousands set against him. He asks the LORD to arise and save him, recalls that the LORD has struck his enemies and broken the teeth of the wicked, and closes by declaring that salvation belongs to the LORD and asking for blessing on his people.

The LORD is described by David as a shield around him, his glory, and the one who lifts up his head. He answers David's cry from his holy hill and sustains him through sleep and waking. David asks him to arise and save him, says he has struck all of David's enemies on the cheek bone and broken the teeth of the wicked, and declares that salvation belongs to him.

David, fleeing from his son Absalom, laments that his adversaries have increased and that some say there is no help for him in God. He trusts the LORD as shield and sustainer, cries out to him, sleeps and wakes safely, and says he will not fear tens of thousands against him. He calls on the LORD to arise and save him and asks for blessing on the LORD's people.

David's adversaries have increased and many rise up against him, and many say of him that there is no help for him in God. They are said to have set themselves against him on every side in tens of thousands. David says the LORD has struck all his enemies on the cheek bone and broken the teeth of the wicked.

Chapter 4 is a psalm by David, addressed to the Chief Musician and set for stringed instruments. David calls on God, the God of his righteousness, to answer him, relieve his distress, and show mercy. He then turns to the sons of men, asking how long his glory will be turned into dishonor and why they love vanity and seek falsehood. He affirms that the LORD has set apart the godly and hears when he calls, and he urges his hearers to stand in awe, not sin, search their hearts, offer sacrifices of righteousness, and trust the LORD. The psalm ends with David saying the LORD has put gladness in his heart and that he will lie down and sleep in peace, since the LORD alone makes him live in safety.

The LORD is addressed as the God of David's righteousness and is asked to answer, give relief, show mercy, and let the light of his face shine on us. He is said to have set apart the godly for himself, to hear when David calls, to have put gladness in David's heart, and alone to make David live in safety.

David, author of this psalm for the Chief Musician, calls on God for relief from distress and mercy, and complains that his glory is being turned into dishonor. He expresses confidence that the LORD hears him, reports that the LORD has given him gladness, and says he will lie down and sleep in peace and safety.

The sons of men are rebuked by David, who asks how long they will turn his glory into dishonor and love vanity and seek falsehood. They are urged to stand in awe, not sin, search their hearts on their beds and be still, offer sacrifices of righteousness, and trust the LORD.

Chapter 5 is a psalm by David, addressed to the Chief Musician with the flutes, in which the psalmist prays to the LORD, his King and God, asking to be heard in the morning. He affirms that the LORD does not delight in wickedness and will destroy liars, the arrogant, the bloodthirsty and the deceitful. The psalmist says he will enter God's house through God's loving kindness and bow toward the holy temple. He asks the LORD to lead him in righteousness and make his way straight because of his enemies, whom he describes as unfaithful, destructive and flattering. He asks God to hold them guilty and thrust them out, and he closes by saying those who take refuge in God will rejoice and the righteous will be surrounded with favor like a shield.

The LORD is addressed as King and God and is asked to hear the psalmist's prayer in the morning. He takes no pleasure in wickedness, hates workers of iniquity, abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful, and will destroy those who speak lies. He is asked to lead the psalmist in righteousness and to hold the enemies guilty, and he is said to defend those who take refuge in him and to bless the righteous, surrounding them with favor as with a shield.

Chapter 6 is a psalm by David, addressed to the LORD and written for the Chief Musician on stringed instruments, upon the eight-stringed lyre. David pleads not to be rebuked or disciplined in the LORD's anger, asking for mercy and healing because he is faint, his bones are troubled, and his soul is in great anguish. He appeals to the LORD to return, deliver him, and save him for the sake of his loving kindness, noting that in death and Sheol there is no memory of or thanks to the LORD. David describes his weariness, nightly weeping, and eyes wasted by grief because of his adversaries. He then turns to address the workers of iniquity, declaring that the LORD has heard his weeping and accepted his prayer, and he asks that his enemies be ashamed, dismayed, and suddenly disgraced.

The LORD is addressed by David, who asks him not to rebuke or discipline him in anger and wrath, and to show mercy, heal, return, deliver, and save for the sake of his loving kindness. David states that the LORD has heard the voice of his weeping and his supplication, and that the LORD accepts his prayer.

David, author of this psalm, pleads with the LORD for mercy and healing, describing himself as faint, with troubled bones, a soul in great anguish, and nightly tears that flood his bed. He asks to be saved, telling the LORD that the dead in Sheol cannot give thanks. He ends confident that the LORD has heard his weeping and accepted his prayer, and he asks that his enemies be disgraced.

David's adversaries are the cause of his grief, which makes his eye waste away and grow old. David commands these workers of iniquity to depart from him, and asks that they be ashamed, dismayed, turned back, and suddenly disgraced.

l: suffering and anguish (David's illness and grief), Psalms, Chapter 6
s: David's suffering is described as faintness, troubled bones, great anguish of soul, weariness from groaning, and nightly weeping that floods his bed and drenches his couch. His eye wastes away and grows old with grief because of his adversaries. He asks the LORD for healing and relief, and ends by affirming that the LORD has heard his weeping.

David's prayer in this psalm consists of pleas that the LORD not rebuke him in anger, that he have mercy, heal, return, deliver, and save him, and that his enemies be shamed. He argues that the dead cannot remember or thank the LORD. The psalm closes with David declaring that the LORD has heard his supplication and accepts his prayer.
